⚡️🇮🇱 — BIG: An Israeli N12 investigation has alleged that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office helped orchestrate the Election Day arrests of three Arab political activists to fuel claims that Arabs were stealing the election, according to The Jerusalem Post and Ynet.
➡️ Netanyahu's chief of staff, Ido Norden, reportedly called police the day before the election and directed them to a purported intelligence source — a former Prime Minister's Office employee close to ex-director-general Yossi Shelley. The information he provided led to raids and arrests without warrants on Election Day, and later proved unfounded. Investigators are examining whether the intelligence was deliberately planted.
➡️ The report also says Shin Bet chief David Zini sought to wiretap five Arab lawmakers over suspected foreign election interference, but the Attorney General's office blocked the request. Zini reportedly told opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot two days after the vote that he had evidence dating back to 2018 of Arabs "stealing elections" that previous Shin Bet chiefs had ignored.
➡️ Netanyahu repeatedly amplified news of the arrests throughout Election Day, and his office has dismissed the report as "false" and "grounds for defamation," insisting Norden merely connected a source with criminal information to police.

🌏 Gulf oil pivots to Asia: How the Hormuz crisis is redrawing the global energy map
As attacks on UAE and Saudi oil infrastructure turn the Strait of Hormuz into a combat zone, Gulf producers and Asian consumers are fundamentally restructuring the global energy supply chain by building reserves directly in Southeast Asia.
🔶 Before the conflict, over half of Southeast Asia’s crude and 90% of Japan’s oil came from the Persian Gulf.
🔶 With oil >$100 a barrel and shipping lanes threatened by mines and missiles, relying on long-haul tankers is no longer viable.
🔶 Saudi Arabia and the UAE are now backing a Japan-led initiative to store oil reserves across ASEAN nations, including Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines.
By shifting reserves to Asia, Gulf states seek to secure guaranteed market access without risking their tankers in contested waters, while Asian nations buffer themselves against supply shocks.
The Gulf's economic future is being firmly anchored to Asia. By physically relocating their oil reserves eastward, Gulf producers are insulating themselves from Western-led blockades and proving that the "West Asian New Order" is inextricably linked to the East.

events.text:
🇺🇸🚀 40 Amazon satellites wiped out as US rocket suffers mission failure
A United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan rocket suffered an anomaly around 10 minutes after liftoff from Cape Canaveral, failing to deliver its payload of 40 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit.
The cause of the malfunction remains unclear, with ULA and engine supplier Blue Origin expected to investigate.
The failure is another setback for Amazon's efforts to challenge SpaceX's Starlink network, as launch disruptions continue to delay deployment of its satellite constellation.
🔴 The incident is particularly damaging for ULA, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, which had touted a 100% mission success record since its formation in 2006
🔴 It was only Vulcan's fifth flight since its 2024 debut - previous technical investigations into its solid rocket boosters and BE-4 engines had already delayed its launch schedule
🔴 Latest failure could trigger another lengthy grounding, further tightening US launch capacity 
🔴 ULA had also yet to regain full approval for national security launches following earlier booster problems
Amazon has deployed 398 Leo satellites across 14 launches since 2025, just 12% of the 3,236 required for global coverage. 
SpaceX, by comparison, operates a network of more than 11,000 Starlink satellites, and, unlike Amazon, controls its own launch infrastructure rather than depending on outside providers.
